title: Light and emission spectra
html:
Guiding question

How can we model the energy states of electrons in atoms?

This question has many layers. What are electrons? How do we know they exist in energy states? What models of these energy states are there?

According to modern views, electrons are quantum objects that behave as both particles and waves. This has no analogue in everyday life, but we can picture electrons in atoms as fuzzy clouds. The shapes and sizes of these clouds depend on the energies of the electrons, which can have only certain, predefined values. The evidence for all of this starts with light.

Understandings (Structure 1.3)

CodeUnderstanding
1.3.1Emission spectra are produced by atoms emitting photons when electrons in excited states return to lower energy levels.
1.3.2The line emission spectrum of hydrogen provides evidence for the existence of electrons in discrete energy levels, which converge at higher energies.
1.3.3The main energy level is given an integer number, n, and can hold a maximum of 2n² electrons.
1.3.4A more detailed model of the atom describes the division of the main energy level into s, p, d and f sublevels of successively higher energies.
1.3.5Each orbital has a defined energy state for a given electron configuration and chemical environment, and can hold two electrons of opposite spin. Sublevels contain a fixed number of orbitals, regions of space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
1.3.6 (AHL)In an emission spectrum, the limit of convergence at higher frequency corresponds to ionization.
1.3.7 (AHL)Successive ionization energy data for an element give information about its electron configuration.

Do now: what makes us see something in colour, or as black or white? An object looks red because it absorbs the other colours of white light and reflects (or emits) red. A black object absorbs nearly all visible light; a white one reflects nearly all of it. Colour is information about which wavelengths of light are absorbed or given out, and that is exactly the tool chemists use to probe electrons.

The electromagnetic spectrum

Visible light is one type of electromagnetic (EM) radiation. The EM spectrum also includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared (IR), ultraviolet (UV), X-rays and gamma rays. A copy of the EM spectrum is in your data booklet.

  • The energy of radiation is inversely proportional to its wavelength, λ: E ∝ 1/λ.
  • All EM waves travel at the speed of light, c ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, in a vacuum.
  • Wavelength and frequency, f (also written ν), are related by c = f × λ, so they are inversely proportional.
  • High-energy waves (e.g. gamma rays) have short wavelengths and high frequencies; low-energy waves (e.g. microwaves) have long wavelengths and low frequencies.
E ∝ 1λc = f × λ
Region (low to high energy)Approx. frequency / HzApprox. wavelength / m
radio wavesbelow 10⁸above 10⁰
microwaves10⁸ to 10¹²10⁰ to 10⁻³
infrared (IR)10¹² to 10¹⁴10⁻⁴ to 7 × 10⁻⁷
visible (red 700 nm to violet 400 nm)about 4 × 10¹⁴ to 7.5 × 10¹⁴7 × 10⁻⁷ to 4 × 10⁻⁷
ultraviolet (UV)10¹⁵ to 10¹⁷4 × 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁹
X-rays10¹⁷ to 10²⁰10⁻⁹ to 10⁻¹²
gamma rays (γ)above 10²⁰below 10⁻¹²

Within the visible region: red has the longest wavelength (about 700 nm), then orange, yellow, green (about 500 to 550 nm), blue, and violet has the shortest (about 400 nm). Visible light spans 400 nm to 700 nm.

Common mistake"Infrared has more energy than visible light" or "visible light has a shorter wavelength than UV": both wrong. Remember: violet is next to UV and higher in energy than red.
ActivityCompare red and green light. Which has (a) the higher wavelength, (b) the higher frequency, (c) the higher energy? (Red: longer wavelength. Green: higher frequency and higher energy.)

Calculate the frequency of red light of wavelength 700 nm (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹).

Convert to metres first: 700 nm = 700 × 10⁻⁹ m = 7.00 × 10⁻⁷ m.
f = c ÷ λ = 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 7.00 × 10⁻⁷ = 4.29 × 10¹⁴ Hz (s⁻¹).

Continuous and line spectra (Structure 1.3.1)

Much of our understanding of electron configurations comes from studying how atoms interact with light.

  • In the 1600s Isaac Newton showed that sunlight can be split into different colours with a prism. This gives a continuous spectrum: light of all wavelengths (frequencies, energies) in a range, a continuous series of colours where each colour merges into the next with no gaps. Classic example: the rainbow.
  • A pure gaseous element at reduced pressure glows (emits light) when a high voltage is applied. Passed through a prism, this light gives a series of coloured lines on a dark background: an emission spectrum, a line spectrum containing only certain, specific wavelengths.
  • When a cold gas is placed between the prism and a source of visible light of all wavelengths, a series of dark lines appears within a continuous spectrum: an absorption spectrum.
SpectrumSourceWhat is seen
continuousvisible light of all wavelengths (light bulb, the Sun) through a prismunbroken band of colours from red to violet
emissionhot (excited) gas through a prisma few bright coloured lines on a black background
absorptionwhite light passing through a cold gas, then a prismcontinuous spectrum crossed by dark lines (at the same positions as the emission lines of that gas)

Emission spectra are produced when atoms emit photons as electrons in excited states return to lower energy levels. The aurora borealis (Northern Lights) is a natural example: charged high-energy particles from the Sun are drawn by the Earth's magnetic field to the polar regions, where they excite atoms and molecules of atmospheric gases, causing them to emit light.

Every element has its own line spectrum

Each element has its own characteristic line spectrum, which can be used to identify it, like a barcode identifies a product or a fingerprint identifies a person. Example: excited sodium atoms emit yellow-orange light at 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm: sodium streetlights glow that colour, and the sodium line spectrum is just two close yellow lines. The same yellow-orange colour appears in a flame test of any sodium-containing substance. Helium was discovered in the Sun (helios) from its spectrum before it was ever found on Earth.

Nature of science · ObservationsChemists generate data by observing properties of matter, either directly with the senses (often sight) or with instruments. Advances in technology extend our observations, revealing features that are otherwise imperceptible. Sodium vapour lamps emit orange-yellow light; a spectroscope shows a strong emission in the yellow region. Helium lamps also look orange to the naked eye, but the helium emission spectrum is more complex, with many lines. Question: what is the difference between observing a natural phenomenon directly and with the aid of an instrument?

Which element is the unknown sample (spectrum 1)?

  1. Beryllium
  2. Copper
  3. Manganese
  4. Strontium

The unknown has a line near 415 nm, three close blue lines between about 435 and 450 nm, and three orange-red lines at about 610, 640 and 660 nm: an exact match, line for line, with strontium (spectrum 5). Strontium salts give fireworks their red colour.

Flame tests and fireworks

Practical · Flame testsFlame testing is an analytical technique to identify some metals. The principle is atomic emission: electrons are promoted to a higher energy level by the heat of the flame; when they fall back to a lower level, photons of certain wavelengths are emitted, some in the visible region.
Flame colours: zinc pale yellow-white (often hard to see), potassium lilac, strontium red, sodium orange-yellow, copper blue-green, lithium red (crimson), calcium orange-red.
Relevant skills: Inquiry 2: identify and record relevant qualitative observations.
Safety: eye protection; precautions around open flames; dilute hydrochloric acid is an irritant; some chloride salts are irritants, avoid skin contact; dispose of all substances appropriately; follow teacher's further precautions.
Materials: flame test wire (platinum or nichrome); dilute HCl; Bunsen burner and heatproof mat; samples of metal salts (e.g. LiCl, NaCl, KCl, CaCl₂, SrCl₂, CuCl₂).
Method: (1) Clean the wire by dipping it in HCl and holding it in a non-luminous flame; repeat until no flame colour is seen. (2) Dip the wire in a salt sample, place it in the edge of the non-luminous flame, record the metal and colour(s). (3) Clean the wire and repeat with other salts. (4) Clear up as instructed.
Questions: (1) Look up the emission spectra of the metals tested, compare with the colours observed, comment on similarities and differences. (2) Explain why different metals show different flame colours.
Explain why different metals give different flame colours

Each element has a different nuclear charge and electron arrangement, so its energy levels are at different energies. The energy gaps between levels are therefore different, so the photons emitted when electrons fall back have different energies, which means different frequencies and wavelengths (E = hf = hc/λ). The colour we see is the mixture of the visible wavelengths emitted.

TOK · Inductive and deductive reasoningKnowledge is developed through reasoning, which can be inductive or deductive.
Inductive reasoning ("bottom-up"): observation → pattern → hypothesis → theory. Specific observations build general principles. Example: LiCl, lithium sulfate and LiI all give red flame tests, so all lithium salts give red flame tests.
Deductive reasoning ("top-down"): theory → hypothesis → pattern → observation. Specific conclusions are inferred from general premises, as when applying scientific knowledge in a new context. Example: lithium bromide is a lithium salt; lithium salts give red flame tests; so lithium bromide gives a red flame test.
Questions: What are the advantages and disadvantages of each type? Can reasoning always be neatly classified into these two types? On what grounds might we doubt a claim reached by induction? By deduction?

Reading the light of stars

Most of what we know about the physical nature of stars comes from spectroscopy. A star's temperature, pressure, composition and even velocity can be worked out from its spectrum. The hot interior gives a continuous spectrum; cooler gas in the star's outer layers absorbs particular wavelengths, leaving dark lines.

Data-based questionThe hydrogen emission spectrum has bright lines at about 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm. The absorption spectrum of the Sun (a continuous spectrum from 390 to 760 nm) has many dark lines. Explain how we know that stars are partly composed of hydrogen. (Dark lines in the Sun's spectrum appear at exactly the wavelengths of the hydrogen emission lines, so hydrogen in the Sun's outer layers is absorbing those wavelengths.)

What kind of spectrum would you expect from the atmosphere of a star viewed in visible light?

  1. An absorption spectrum: a continuous spectrum with dark lines
  2. A continuous spectrum only
  3. An emission spectrum: bright lines on black
  4. No spectrum, because the atmosphere is transparent

Light from the hot interior passes through the cooler atmosphere, whose atoms absorb their characteristic wavelengths, leaving dark lines.

title: The hydrogen spectrum and energy levels
html:
Structure 1.3.2 Photons and quantization

Each line in an emission spectrum has a specific wavelength, corresponding to a specific amount of energy. This is quantization: EM radiation comes in discrete packets, or quanta. A photon is a quantum of energy, proportional to the frequency of the radiation:

E = h × f
  • E = energy of the photon, in joules (J)
  • h = Planck's constant, 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (data booklet)
  • f = frequency, in hertz (Hz) or s⁻¹

Combining with c = fλ gives E = hc/λ.

Calculate the energy of one photon of the red hydrogen line, λ = 656 nm.

λ = 656 × 10⁻⁹ m = 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ m.
E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) ÷ 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ = 3.03 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per photon.

Explaining the hydrogen spectrum

When hydrogen gas in a discharge tube is excited and its light is passed through a slit and a prism, we see a line spectrum, not a continuous spectrum. The visible part has just four lines.

The explanation, in three steps:

  1. Electrons in hydrogen absorb energy (from the electric discharge, heat or a photon of exactly the right energy) and "jump up" to a higher energy level. The electron is now excited.
  2. The excited state is unstable. Attracted by the nucleus, the electron "falls" back down to a lower energy level and emits the excess energy as a photon of EM radiation.
  3. Only certain energies of light are seen, so the energy difference between any two levels must be a fixed amount. The energy of the light emitted directly reflects the spacing between the levels.
Exam tip · explaining a line spectrum (3 marks)(1) Electrons absorb energy and are promoted (excited) to higher energy levels. (2) They fall back to lower levels and emit the difference in energy as a photon. (3) Energy levels are fixed (quantised), so only specific energy differences are possible → only specific frequencies/wavelengths → lines. Converging lines at higher energy show that energy levels get closer together further from the nucleus.

The Bohr model (1913)

Niels Bohr proposed a model of the hydrogen atom based on its emission spectrum. Main postulates:

  1. The electron can exist only in certain stationary orbits around the nucleus, associated with discrete energy levels.
  2. When an electron in the lowest orbit absorbs a photon of the right energy, it moves to a higher energy level and stays there for a short time.
  3. When the electron returns to a lower level, it emits a photon whose energy equals the energy difference between the two levels.

Bohr's theory was the first attempt to fix the main problem of the Rutherford model (Structure 1.2): classical electrodynamics predicted orbiting electrons would radiate energy and quickly fall into the nucleus, so atoms could not exist for long. Bohr postulated that electrons do not radiate energy while in stationary orbits.

Because electrons could only have certain energies, transitions between orbits absorb or emit photons of specific wavelengths, giving the characteristic lines. Measuring the wavelengths allowed the electron energies to be calculated. For hydrogen:

En = −RH × 1n²RH ≈ 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J (Rydberg constant)
  • This equation shows the quantum nature of the atom: electron energy has only discrete, quantized values. The energies are negative because zero is defined as the electron completely removed from the atom (n = ∞).
  • These values are characterized by integer or half-integer parameters called quantum numbers.
  • The principal quantum number (n) takes only positive integer values (1, 2, 3, ...); greater n means higher energy.

Ground and excited states

  • The ground state is the most stable state, n = 1 for hydrogen, where the electron has the lowest possible energy and is closest to the nucleus.
  • Levels with n = 2, 3, ... are excited states: higher energy, further from the nucleus, temporary and unstable. Atoms in excited states spontaneously return to the ground state by emitting photons of specific wavelengths.
  • An electron absorbs energy (excitation) and moves to a higher orbit; it then falls back (decay), emitting a photon of energy hf.
  • Energy levels are like a ladder with unevenly spaced rungs. Electrons cannot exist between levels. Jumping up a level needs a specific, discrete amount of energy; jumping down releases the same amount.

Visible lines of hydrogen (Balmer series, transitions to n = 2)

An electron can be excited to any level and return to any lower level. Transitions down to n = 2 give the visible lines:

ColourWavelength / nmTransition
red656n = 3 → n = 2
cyan (blue-green)486n = 4 → n = 2
blue (blue-violet)434n = 5 → n = 2
violet410n = 6 → n = 2

The red line has a longer wavelength and lower frequency than the violet line: the photon released for n = 3 → 2 has less energy than for n = 6 → 2. Each line is the difference between two allowed energy states of the electron.

Series in the hydrogen spectrum

Electron falls toSeriesRegionEnergy
n = 1Lymanultraviolethighest
n = 2Balmervisibleintermediate
n = 3Pascheninfraredlowest
  • Transitions to n = 1 (ground state) release the most energy: short-wavelength ultraviolet lines.
  • Transitions to n = 2: visible lines.
  • Transitions to n = 3: infrared lines.
  • The allowed energy levels get closer together (converge) further from the nucleus. The gap between n = 3 and n = 2 is much smaller than between n = 2 and n = 1. So lines within each series also get closer together at higher frequency, converging at the high-frequency (short-wavelength) end.
  • Electrons absorb or release only the exact energy needed to move between allowed states. Excess energy is not absorbed; if too little energy is supplied the electron does not move.
  • Emission = a fall (higher n → lower n). A transition upwards (e.g. n = 1 → 2) is absorption, not emission: a common multiple-choice trap.
  • Longest wavelength = smallest energy gap, e.g. n = 3 → 2 (the red Balmer line). Highest energy = the largest gap, e.g. n = ∞ → 1.

Which statements are correct for the emission spectrum of hydrogen? I. The lines converge at higher frequencies. II. Electron transitions to n = 2 are responsible for lines in the visible region. III. Lines are produced when electrons move from lower to higher energy levels.

  1. I and II only
  2. I and III only
  3. II and III only
  4. I, II and III

III describes absorption, not emission: emission lines come from electrons falling from higher to lower levels.

Which transition in a hydrogen atom emits the photon of longest wavelength?

  1. n = 2 → n = 1
  2. n = 4 → n = 2
  3. n = 3 → n = 2
  4. n = 1 → n = 3

Longest wavelength = lowest energy = smallest gap. Of the emissions, 3 → 2 is the smallest gap (the red line). n = 1 → 3 is an absorption, not an emission.

Maximum electrons in a main energy level (Structure 1.3.3)

Energy levels closer to the nucleus hold fewer electrons. The maximum number of electrons in level n is 2n².

nMaximum electrons (2n²)
12
28
318
432

What is the maximum number of electrons the n = 5 level could hold?

2n² = 2 × 5² = 2 × 25 = 50.

An element's highest occupied main energy level is the same as its period number: sodium, in period 3, has its outer electron in n = 3.

Practical: observing emission spectra

Spectrometers and spectroscopes are devices for dispersing light into its constituent colours using prisms and/or diffraction gratings.

Practical · Emission spectraEmission spectra can be observed with a simple handheld spectroscope held up to a light source. Discharge lamps contain low-pressure gases that are ionized when a voltage is applied: electrons flow and collide with the gas atoms, exciting them into higher energy levels; returning to lower levels, the atoms emit photons of specific energies.
Aim: to see spectral lines from different elements in emission and absorption.
Relevant skills: Tool 3: construct graphs and draw lines of best fit. Inquiry 2: identify and record relevant qualitative observations and sufficient relevant quantitative data; identify and describe patterns, trends and relationships; assess accuracy.
Safety: wear eye protection; discharge lamps get very hot, handle with care; follow further precautions from your teacher for the specific lamps.
Materials: discharge lamps (e.g. hydrogen, helium, neon, mercury, CO₂); handheld spectroscope; coloured pencils.
Method: (1) Observe natural light through the spectroscope and note the spectrum. (2) Observe artificial light from a computer screen or LED and note the spectrum. (3) Observe light from various discharge lamps; note the overall colour of each tube, then use coloured pencils to draw each line at its accurate position on a 350 to 750 nm scale.
Questions: (1) Sketch the spectra observed. (2) Describe each as continuous, emission or absorption. (3) Look up the emission spectra of the elements in the lamps; compare theoretical and observed lines (number, colours, positions). (4) Plot theoretical wavelength against observed wavelength with a line of best fit. (5) Comment on the relationship shown. (6) Comment on the accuracy of the observed wavelengths. (7) How could this information identify unknown substances? (8) What does it show about energy levels? (9) Which colour of visible light has the lowest energy, and which energy levels would it relate to? (Red; in hydrogen, the small n = 3 → 2 gap.)
ATL · Communication skillsDiagrams, graphs and images help convey ideas. Write an explanation of atomic emission without any diagrams. Swap with a partner and give feedback on: use of scientific vocabulary, the order of ideas, and whether important concepts are missing. Improve your work using the feedback, then choose a graph, image or diagram to accompany it and discuss why you chose it and whether it adds to the explanation.

Emission lines are produced when electrons fall from higher to lower energy levels; the lines converge at higher frequency because the energy levels get closer together.

Linking questionsWhat qualitative and quantitative data can be collected from instruments such as gas discharge tubes and prisms in the study of emission spectra from gaseous elements and from light? (Inquiry 2)
How do emission spectra provide evidence for the existence of different elements? (Structure 1.2)
How does an element's highest occupied main energy level relate to its period number in the periodic table? (Structure 3.1)

title: Orbitals and sublevels
html:
The quantum mechanical model of the atom (Structure 1.3.4)

The Bohr model tried to explain the energy states of electrons using quantization: electrons exist in discrete energy levels. Hydrogen's emission spectrum consists of narrow lines because their wavelengths correspond to differences between allowed energy levels. However, the model had several problems and incorrect assumptions.

Limitations of the Bohr model

  1. It could not predict the emission spectra of elements with more than one electron; it only worked for hydrogen.
  2. It assumed the electron was a subatomic particle in a fixed orbit around the nucleus.
  3. It could not account for the effect of electric and magnetic fields on the spectral lines of atoms and ions.
  4. It could not explain molecular bonding and geometry (covered in Structure 2.2).
  5. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle says the location and momentum of an electron cannot both be known precisely at the same time. Bohr's model stated electrons had fixed momentum in specific circular orbits.

Because of these limitations the Bohr theory was superseded by the modern quantum mechanical model of the atom.

Which is a limitation of the Bohr model?

  1. It cannot explain the line spectrum of hydrogen
  2. It cannot predict the spectra of atoms with more than one electron
  3. It does not include a nucleus
  4. It says energy levels are quantized

Bohr's model explains hydrogen's spectrum very well, and quantization is its great success. It fails for every atom with more than one electron.

TOK · Quantum mechanics and the limits of knowledgeModern quantum mechanics combines quantization with these key principles.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: it is impossible to determine accurately both the momentum and the position of a particle simultaneously. The more we know about an electron's position, the less we know about its momentum, and vice versa. We cannot pinpoint an electron or predict its trajectory, but we can calculate the probability of finding it in each region of space.
"One aim of the physical sciences has been to give an exact picture of the material world. One achievement ... has been to prove that this aim is unattainable." Jacob Bronowski (1908–1974). What are the implications of the uncertainty principle for the boundaries of knowledge? What are the limits of human knowledge?
Wave–particle duality: electrons and other subatomic species behave as both particles and waves. Mass, momentum and being absorbed or released as discrete entities suggest particles. But photons, electrons and even whole atoms and small molecules show interference (combination of waveforms), diffraction (bending around obstacles) and tunnelling (passing through obstacles), which are wave properties.
"We have two contradictory pictures of reality; separately neither of them fully explains the phenomena of light, but together they do." Albert Einstein (1879–1955).
Wave–particle duality of the electron is described quantitatively by the Schrödinger equation (1926, Erwin Schrödinger, Austria). Its solutions are three-dimensional mathematical functions called wave functions, which describe the possible states and energies of electrons in atoms.
Wave–particle duality shows that objects of study do not always fit neatly into our categories. What is the role of categorization in constructing knowledge?

Shells, sublevels and orbitals

Three words, nested inside each other:

  • Electrons are arranged in shells (main energy levels, numbered by n).
  • Each shell is split into sublevels (sub-shells): s, p, d and f.
  • Each sublevel is made of orbitals, each of which can hold 2 electrons.
  • Schrödinger's wave functions describe electrons in terms of probability density, using Heisenberg's idea that momentum and position are uncertain. Instead of a defined path, the theory gives the probability of finding an electron in a region of space at a certain distance from the nucleus.
  • An atomic orbital is a region in space where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
  • Each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons and has a characteristic shape and energy.
  • The first four orbital types, in order of increasing energy, are s, p, d and f. Later ones are theoretical and labelled alphabetically (g, h, i, k and so on).
  • The principal quantum number n (from the Bohr model) gives the main energy levels. These are split into sublevels made of atomic orbitals. For n = 1, 2 and 3 the s orbitals are 1s, 2s and 3s. As n increases, the s orbital is further from the nucleus.

s orbitals

An s orbital is spherical. The sphere drawn is the boundary enclosing a 99% probability of finding the electron. An s orbital holds two electrons.

Plots of probability against distance from the nucleus for the first three s orbitals show how they grow:

OrbitalProbability with distance from nucleusRegions of zero probability (nodes)
1sHighest probability close to the nucleus; falls off further out but never reaches zeronone
2sHighest probability further out than 1s, with a small probability closer to the nucleus (small inner peak)one, between the two peaks
3sHighest probability at an even greater distance, with two smaller inner peakstwo

So each s orbital is larger than the one before (1s < 2s < 3s): electrons in higher main levels are, on average, further from the nucleus. (For hydrogen, the most probable distance of the 1s electron from the nucleus is about 53 pm.)

An analogy: where is the teacher?

A teacher is late for an 8.00 am lesson. At 8.15 students suggest they could be in the staff room, lab or library; the principal's office or car park; at home in town; at the airport; or even the North Pole. The exact location is unknown, but you could draw a 3D cluster of dots where the probability of finding the teacher is high, and draw a boundary enclosing a 99% chance (the school perimeter, the town, or a region including the airport). An atomic orbital likewise represents the region with a high probability of finding an electron.

A 1s orbital can be drawn as a cluster of dots (densest at the nucleus) or as a sphere enclosing 99% of the dots.

p orbitals

  • A p orbital is dumbbell shaped (two lobes).
  • There are three p orbitals, oriented parallel to the x, y and z axes: px, py and pz.
  • There is zero probability of finding the electron at the intersection of the axes, between the two lobes.
  • Each p orbital holds two electrons.

Which describes a 2p orbital?

  1. Spherical, holding up to 6 electrons
  2. Dumbbell-shaped, holding up to 6 electrons
  3. Dumbbell-shaped, holding up to 2 electrons
  4. Spherical, holding up to 2 electrons

Every orbital, whatever its shape, holds at most 2 electrons. The 2p sublevel (three p orbitals) holds 6.

Orbital types and energy

  • Each orbital type has a characteristic shape and energy.
  • The s orbital is spherical and has the lowest energy. There is one s orbital per level.
  • There are three p orbitals, each oriented differently.
  • There are five d and seven f orbitals, higher in energy than s or p.
  • Only the shapes of s and p orbitals need to be known.

Each energy level n contains n types of orbital (sublevels): n = 1 only s; n = 2 s and p; n = 3 s, p and d; n = 4 s, p, d and f. Level n has n² orbitals and holds up to 2n² electrons.

nSublevelOrbitals per typeTotal orbitals (n²)Max electrons (2n²)
1s112
2s, p1, 348
3s, p, d1, 3, 5918
4s, p, d, f1, 3, 5, 71632

Table 1 example: n = 4 has four orbital types (s, p, d, f), 16 orbitals in total, holding a maximum of 2(4)² = 32 electrons.

ActivityFor the energy level with n = 5, state: (a) the sublevel types; (b) the number of atomic orbitals in each sublevel; (c) the total number of atomic orbitals; (d) the maximum number of electrons at that energy level.
Answer for n = 5

Level n has n sublevels and n² orbitals, holding 2n² electrons. For n = 5: 5s, 5p, 5d, 5f and 5g with 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9 orbitals; 25 orbitals; 50 electrons. Only 5s, 5p, 5d and 5f are occupied in known ground-state atoms.

How many atomic orbitals are there in the n = 3 level?

n² = 3² = 9: one 3s + three 3p + five 3d.
Nature of science · Theories and modelsCurrent atomic theory evolved from earlier models, each superseding the one before. Theories are comprehensive systems of ideas that model and explain an aspect of the natural world. Unlike everyday use of "theory", scientific theories are backed by vast amounts of observations and tested hypotheses, gathered, documented and communicated by many scientists.
Timeline: 800–400 BCE Āruni's kana and Democritus' atomos (indivisible particles); 1803 Dalton's "billiard ball" model; 1897 Thomson's "plum pudding" model; 1911–12 Rutherford's nuclear model; 1913 Bohr model; 1926 Heisenberg's uncertainty and regions of probability model; 1930 quantum mechanical model. Atoms evolved from indestructible spheres to a model where electrons have specific energies and are found in regions of high probability.
Question: What other examples of theories can you think of?
Linking questionWhat is the relationship between energy sublevels and the block nature of the periodic table? (Structure 3.1)

title: Electron configurations
html:
Structure 1.3.5 Orbital diagrams

Do now: how many electrons fit in each shell? What are the electron configurations of neon and calcium, and which is more reactive? By convention, an "arrow in box" notation called an orbital diagram shows how electrons are arranged in atomic orbitals. The arrangement of electrons in orbitals is called the electron configuration. Each box represents one orbital; arrows in the boxes represent electrons; each box holds a maximum of two arrows.

SublevelNumber of boxes (orbitals)Maximum electrons
s12
p (pₓ, p_y, p_z)36
d510
f714

Electron spin and the Pauli exclusion principle

Atomic orbitals are regions of space with a high probability of finding electrons. Electrons are negatively charged and repel each other, so two electrons should not be able to occupy the same region of space. Quantum mechanics solves this by giving each electron a ± spin. A pair of electrons with opposite spins behaves like two magnets facing in opposite directions.

Electron spin is shown by a half-arrow pointing up (positive spin, ↿) or down (negative spin, ⇂). Two electrons of opposite spin in one orbital are drawn as ↿⇂ in one box, like two bar magnets placed N-to-S.

Pauli exclusion principle: only two electrons can occupy the same atomic orbital and those electrons must have opposite spins.

TOKElectron spin is often interpreted as rotation of the electron around its own axis ("one electron spins clockwise and one anticlockwise"). This has no physical basis: electrons in atoms behave like waves, and a wave cannot rotate. Neither spin nor wave-like behaviour can be visualized, as they have no analogue in everyday life and can only be expressed mathematically. This does not undermine quantum theory; it shows the limits of human perception and the power of mathematics as the language of science. To what extent does mathematics support knowledge development in the natural sciences?

Degenerate orbitals and Hund's rule

The atomic orbitals of the same type within one sublevel all have equal energy. Orbitals with the same energy are called degenerate orbitals. The three 2p orbitals are degenerate; the three 3p orbitals are degenerate; the five 3d orbitals are degenerate. The 2p orbitals are lower in energy than the 3p orbitals. Energy order: 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 3d (for a one-electron atom); in many-electron atoms 4s drops just below 3d.

Boron (5 electrons): 1s² 2s² 2p¹. Orbital diagram: 1s ↿⇂, 2s ↿⇂, 2p ↿ _ _. The single 2p electron can occupy any of the three degenerate 2p orbitals. Degenerate orbitals are drawn as joined boxes to show they have equal energy. Traditionally the arrow goes in the leftmost box, but this is personal preference.

Hund's rule: every degenerate orbital in a sublevel is singly occupied before any orbital is doubly occupied, and all electrons in singly occupied orbitals have the same spin. Like passengers boarding a bus who each take an empty double seat before anyone shares, electrons only pair up when no empty orbital of the same energy is left.

Nitrogen, 1s² 2s² 2p³: the correct diagram is 2p ↿ ↿ ↿ (one electron in each 2p orbital, parallel spins). 2p ↿⇂ ↿ _ is incorrect (pairing before every orbital is singly filled).

Aufbau principle

Aufbau principle: as electrons are added to atoms, the lowest available energy orbitals fill before higher energy orbitals do ("Aufbau" is German for "building up").

The third and fourth energy levels contain d and f orbitals. These are typically filled after the s orbitals of the following level because they are higher in energy. The 3d sublevel is higher in energy than 4s but lower than 4p, so 4s fills first, then 3d, then 4p. For the same reason 4d fills after 5s, and 4f fills only after 6s.

This agrees with experimental data: potassium (K) and calcium (Ca) have their outer electrons in 4s, not 3d. The potassium orbital filling diagram is 1s ↿⇂, 2s ↿⇂, 2p ↿⇂ ↿⇂ ↿⇂, 3s ↿⇂, 3p ↿⇂ ↿⇂ ↿⇂, 4s ↿; the 3d boxes (higher in energy than 4s) stay empty.

General order of filling:

1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d < 4p < 5s < 4d < 5p < 6s < 4f < 5d < 6p …

In the IB Diploma Programme, only electron configurations of atoms and ions up to Z = 36 are assessed (sublevels up to 4p).

Electron sharing and transfer are fundamental to chemical reactions, so it is important to know electron configurations. There are three ways to show them:

  1. Full electron configuration
  2. Condensed electron configuration
  3. Orbital filling diagram ("arrows in boxes")
ActivityComplete orbital diagrams for the ground states of (a) aluminium, Al; (b) chlorine, Cl; (c) iron, Fe. Use the periodic table to find the number of electrons.
Answers: Al, Cl, Fe

Al (13) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹, 3p ↿ _ _
Cl (17) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵, 3p ↿⇂ ↿⇂ ↿
Fe (26) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶, 4s ↿⇂, 3d ↿⇂ ↿ ↿ ↿ ↿

Full electron configurations

To write a full electron configuration, use the periodic table and "build up" electrons in successive orbitals using the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule and the Pauli exclusion principle. The number of electrons in each sublevel is written as a superscript next to the sublevel.

Worked example 1 · Full configuration of calciumDetermine the full electron configuration for the calcium atom.
Ca: Z = 20, so 20 electrons; fill lowest energy first, max 2 per orbital
1s: 2 electrons → 1s²
2s: 2 electrons → 2s²
three 2p orbitals, 2 each → 2p⁶
3s: 2 electrons → 3s²
three 3p orbitals, 2 each → 3p⁶ (18 electrons so far)
2 left go into next lowest orbital, 4s → 4s²
Ca: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s²

Compare neon, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶: every occupied sublevel is full, so neon is unreactive. Calcium has two electrons in 4s beyond a full [Ar] core, which it loses easily, so calcium is far more reactive.

Condensed electron configurations

As atomic number increases, full configurations get long. The chemistry of atoms and ions is mostly determined by their valence electrons (the outermost electrons), not the inner core electrons. A condensed configuration shows the valence electrons and writes the core as the configuration of the previous group 18 element (the noble gases).

Condensed configuration = [previous noble gas] + valence electrons
ElementAtomic numberFull electron configurationCondensed configuration
O81s² 2s² 2p⁴[He] 2s² 2p⁴
Ne101s² 2s² 2p⁶[He] 2s² 2p⁶ (neon's own core is written with [He]; "[Ne]" is the shorthand used for the elements after neon)
Mn251s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁵[Ar] 4s² 3d⁵
Br351s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁵[Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁵

Table 2: examples of full and condensed electron configurations. Writing the sublevels in order of n instead ([Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²) is equally acceptable.

Worked example 2 · Condensed configuration of calciumDetermine the condensed electron configuration for the calcium atom.
Full configuration (worked example 1): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s²
Previous noble gas: argon, Z = 18, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
Ca: [Ar] 4s²

Orbital diagrams can also be condensed:

  • Oxygen: [He] 2s ↿⇂, 2p ↿⇂ ↿ ↿
  • Manganese: [Ar] 4s ↿⇂, 3d ↿ ↿ ↿ ↿ ↿ (five unpaired electrons, same spin)
Practice: write full configurations for sodium, iron, bromine, Rb⁺ and arsenic, and condensed ones for cobalt, magnesium, nitrogen and Sr²⁺
  1. sodium: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹
  2. iron: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶
  3. bromine: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁵
  4. Rb⁺: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁶ (same as krypton)
  5. arsenic: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p³
  6. cobalt: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁷
  7. magnesium: [Ne] 3s²
  8. nitrogen: [He] 2s² 2p³
  9. Sr²⁺: [Kr]
Which elements are these? 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴ · …4p⁶ 5s¹ · [Kr] 5s² 4d¹⁰ 5p³ · [Xe] 6s² 4f¹⁴ 5d⁶ · [Rn] 7s² 5f¹¹

Count the electrons (or find the block position): sulfur (16); rubidium (37); antimony (51); osmium (76); einsteinium (99). Configurations beyond Z = 36 are not examined, but the counting method is the same.

Some configurations fit more than one species: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁶ could be Kr, Br⁻, Se²⁻, Rb⁺ or Sr²⁺ (all isoelectronic, with 36 electrons). [Ar] 4s¹ is potassium (or Ca⁺).

Exceptions: chromium and copper

Their ground-state configurations differ from the Aufbau prediction.

ElementExpected (Aufbau)Observed ground stateReason
Cr (Z = 24)[Ar] 4s² 3d⁴[Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵No paired electrons: six half-occupied orbitals (one 4s, five 3d), all with the same spin
Cu (Z = 29)[Ar] 4s² 3d⁹[Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰A full 3d sublevel

Why? A half-filled (d⁵) or completely filled (d¹⁰) d sublevel, with 4s¹, is lower in energy overall. The electrons in the half-filled d subshell are all unpaired and spread out (less repulsion), so promoting one 4s electron is favourable. Cr and Cu are the only two exceptions you need to know. All other elements up to Z = 36 fill sublevels in the general order.

What is the ground-state configuration of chromium?

  1. [Ar] 4s² 3d⁴
  2. [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵
  3. [Ar] 3d⁶
  4. [Ar] 4s² 4p⁴

Chromium is an exception: a half-filled 3d sublevel plus 4s¹ (six unpaired electrons) is more stable than 4s² 3d⁴.

Ions

When atoms lose electrons to form ions, the electrons in the sublevel with the highest principal quantum number (n) are lost first, even though 4s filled before 3d. Once 3d is occupied, 4s lies above it in energy.

  • Mn is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁵. The 4s electrons are lost first, so Mn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, not [Ar] 4s² 3d³.
  • All elements with 3d valence electrons tend to lose the two 4s electrons to form 2+ ions. These are the 3d transition elements (transition metals), from scandium (Sc) to copper (Cu). Transition metals can also have variable oxidation states in compounds.
  • Exception: scandium has only one 3d electron and readily forms only Sc³⁺, losing its 3d electron and both 4s electrons.
  • Anions gain electrons into the next available orbital: S (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴) becomes S²⁻ (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶).
Key point · transition metal ionsElectrons are removed from the highest occupied main level first. For first-row transition metals, 4s electrons are lost before 3d.
Fe [Ar]3d⁶4s² → Fe²⁺ [Ar]3d⁶ → Fe³⁺ [Ar]3d⁵
Cu [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ → Cu⁺ [Ar]3d¹⁰    Cr [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ → Cr³⁺ [Ar]3d³
Writing Fe²⁺ as [Ar]3d⁴4s² is the classic wrong answer.
ActivityDeduce the electron configuration of the Cu²⁺ cation. (Answer: Cu is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰; remove the 4s electron then one 3d electron: Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹.)

What is the electron configuration of Zn²⁺?

  1. [Ar] 4s² 3d⁸
  2. [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁹
  3. [Ar] 3d¹⁰
  4. [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰

Zn is [Ar] 4s² 3d¹⁰. Both 4s electrons are lost first, leaving [Ar] 3d¹⁰.

Exam questions with mark schemes: try them first

1. Nitrogen forms a nitride ion with configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. (a) Formula of the nitride ion? N³⁻. (b) An ion Q with a single negative charge has the same configuration. Identify Q. F⁻ (fluoride; "fluorine" alone is not accepted). (c) Formula of lithium nitride? Li₃N.

2. An atom of element Z has two more protons and two more neutrons than ³⁴₁₆S. Give its symbol with mass and atomic numbers: ³⁸₁₈Ar. Complete the configurations of S and S²⁻: S 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴; S²⁻ 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶. State and explain the block for sulfur: p-block, because its highest-energy (outer) electrons are in a 3p sublevel (not "2p").

3. Full configurations of Al and Cr³⁺: Al 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹; Cr³⁺ 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d³. The 2+ ion with the same configuration as krypton: Sr²⁺. The compound of a 2+ ion and a 3− ion, both isoelectronic with argon: Ca₃P₂.

Checking whether a configuration is valid

  • No "1p", "2d" or "3f": level n has only n types of sublevel. "4s² 4d¹⁰ 4p⁵" is wrong: after 4s comes 3d.
  • No sublevel holds more than its maximum: s², p⁶, d¹⁰, f¹⁴. "3s³" is impossible.
  • Noble-gas shorthand must use a noble gas in brackets: [Ra] is invalid, and [Xe] cannot be the configuration of xenon itself.
  • Count electrons: the superscripts must add up to Z (atom) or Z − charge (ion).

Which electron configuration is valid?

  1. 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4d¹⁰ 4p⁵
  2. 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s³ 3d⁵
  3. [Ra] 7s² 5f⁸
  4. [Kr] 5s² 4d¹⁰ 5p⁵

(1) has 4d where 3d should be. (2) has 3s³ (an s sublevel holds only 2) and skips 3p. (3) uses radium, which is not a noble gas. (4) is iodine, written correctly.

Unpaired electrons

Use an orbital diagram and Hund's rule. O has 2 unpaired electrons (2p⁴ ↿⇂ ↿ ↿); Fe has 4 (3d⁶); Cr has 6 (3d⁵ 4s¹); Zn and Mg have none.

How many unpaired electrons does a phosphorus atom have in its ground state?

P is [Ne] 3s² 3p³. By Hund's rule the three 3p electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins: 3p ↿ ↿ ↿, so 3 unpaired electrons.

Sublevels and the blocks of the periodic table

Columns of the periodic table are groups (numbered 1 to 18 going across) and rows are periods. The table can be divided into four blocks matching the four sublevels holding the outermost valence electrons:

BlockGroupsOuter sublevel being filled
s-block1 and 2 (plus He, 1s)1s (H, He), 2s, 3s, 4s, 5s, 6s, 7s
d-block (transition elements)3 to 123d (period 4), 4d, 5d, 6d
p-block13 to 182p (period 2) to 7p
f-blockseparate rows below the table4f, 5f

The s-block and p-block together are the main-group elements. Note the d sublevel in a period is one level lower than the period number (period 4 fills 3d), and the f sublevel is two lower (period 6 fills 4f). This is discussed further in Structure 3.1.

When forming ions, transition metals lose their 4s electrons before their 3d electrons; copper and chromium are the two exceptions to the Aufbau order up to Z = 36.

ATL: Self-management skillsThe ideas in this topic range from the quantum mechanical model of the atom to writing electron configurations. Write a chapter summary no longer than one sheet of A4. Write three key takeaways. List the key vocabulary. Write five brief questions testing the ideas, make an answer key, and try them on a peer. (Class plenary: pick a random card numbered 1 to 36 and give the configuration of that element; challenge: predict the charge on its ion too. Why leave out group 14?)
Linking noteIonization and oxidation are covered in Structure 2.1 and Structure 3.1. The periodic table is structured according to the type of sublevel that valence electrons of elements appear in (Structure 3.1).

title: Convergence and ionization energy from spectra
html:
Ionization energy AHL

Do now: what factors would affect how easily an electron can be removed from an atom? Which atom would need the most energy to remove one electron, and which the least? (Helium the most, caesium the least of the common elements: think about distance from the nucleus, nuclear charge and shielding.)

Ionization energy is the minimum energy required to eject an electron out of a neutral atom or molecule in its ground state. The first ionization energy is the energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms in their ground state, producing one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

X(g) → X⁺(g) + e⁻

Gaseous atoms are specified so that the energy measured is only for removing the electron, with no forces between neighbouring atoms to overcome. The process is always endothermic. The quantum mechanical model of the atom explains the trends and discontinuities in the first ionization energies of elements (next lesson). Ionization energy and periodic table trends are discussed further in Structure 3.1.

The convergence limit (Structure 1.3.6) AHL

As the principal quantum number increases, the distance between energy levels decreases until the levels converge to a continuum. This is seen as spectral lines converging in the hydrogen emission spectrum.

Transitions down to level 1 (n = 1) give ultraviolet lines (Lyman series, high energy); transitions down to level 2 give visible lines (Balmer series, lower energy). In each series the lines get closer together at higher energy (shorter wavelength) until they converge.

At the convergence point the levels have merged into a continuum: no extra energy is needed to promote the electron further, because it has left the atom, and the atom has been ionised. We give this limit the principal quantum number n = ∞. For hydrogen (and for any atom whose electron starts in n = 1), the energy needed to promote an electron from n = 1 to n = ∞ is the ionization energy, so the convergence limit of the Lyman series is the shortest wavelength (highest frequency) line in the whole spectrum.

The lines in the hydrogen emission spectrum converge at 9.12 × 10⁻⁸ m (912 Å, 91.2 nm). This is the wavelength of light at which the hydrogen atom is ionized (the electron is removed from n = 1 to n = ∞). The Lyman lines run from about 1215 Å down to 912 Å, getting closer together towards 912 Å.

Why does the convergence limit of the Lyman series correspond to the first ionization energy of hydrogen?

  1. It is the longest-wavelength line in the spectrum
  2. It corresponds to an electron falling from n = 2 to n = 1
  3. It corresponds to the transition between n = ∞ and n = 1, the ground state
  4. All Lyman lines have the same energy

Ionization removes the electron from the ground state (n = 1) completely (n = ∞). The photon for n = ∞ → 1 carries exactly that energy, and it is the shortest-wavelength, highest-frequency line.

Calculating ionization energy from spectral data AHL

The convergence limit wavelength or frequency can be used to calculate the first ionization energy. 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m; 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m.

c = fλE = hfE = hcλIE (kJ mol⁻¹) = E(one atom, J) × NA1000
Data bookletThe speed of light (c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹), Planck's constant (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s) and Avogadro's constant (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) are given in the data booklet. The mole and Avogadro's constant are discussed in Structure 1.4.
  1. Convert the wavelength to metres: nm × 10⁻⁹ ("nano = nine").
  2. f = c ÷ λ (s⁻¹).
  3. E = hf gives the energy to remove the electron from one atom, in J. (Steps 2 and 3 can be combined as E = hc/λ.)
  4. Multiply by NA (6.02 × 10²³) for one mole, then divide by 1000 for kJ mol⁻¹. (The order of these two operations does not matter.)
Worked example 3 · IE of hydrogen from convergenceSpectral lines converge at 9.12 × 10⁻⁸ m in the emission spectrum of hydrogen. Calculate the first ionization energy of hydrogen in kJ mol⁻¹.
c = f × λ: 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ = f × 9.12 × 10⁻⁸ m
f = 3.29 × 10¹⁵ Hz (s⁻¹)
E = h × f = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3.29 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹ = 2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J
(or in one step, E = hc/λ)
This is the energy of one photon that removes one electron from one H atom.
IE = (2.18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) / 1000
IE = 1.31 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹
Worked example 4 · Convergence wavelength of sodiumThe first ionization energy of Na is 496 kJ mol⁻¹ (IB data booklet). Calculate the wavelength of convergence for the sodium atom spectrum in Å.
Energy per atom = 496 000 J mol⁻¹ / 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 8.24 × 10⁻¹⁹ J
E = hc/λ: 8.24 × 10⁻¹⁹ J = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) / λ
λ = 2.41 × 10⁻⁷ m = 2410 Å
This is in the UV region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Worked example · sodium, the other way roundConvergence limit λ = 242 nm.
f = 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 2.42 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.24 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹
E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 1.24 × 10¹⁵ = 8.22 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per atom
IE = 8.22 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 6.02 × 10²³ ÷ 1000 = 495 kJ mol⁻¹ (data booklet: 496)
Common mistakeForgetting NA (an answer around 10⁻²¹ kJ is per atom, not per mole), or forgetting the ÷ 1000. The convergence limit is the shortest wavelength / highest frequency in the Lyman series, n = ∞ → 1, which is why it equals the energy needed to remove the electron from the ground state.

Calculate the first ionization energy of hydrogen if the shortest wavelength in its emission spectrum is 91 nm.

λ = 91 × 10⁻⁹ m = 9.1 × 10⁻⁸ m.
E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) ÷ 9.1 × 10⁻⁸ = 2.19 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom.
IE = 2.19 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 6.02 × 10²³ ÷ 1000 = 1.32 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹ (about 1316).

The convergence limit of hydrogen's Lyman series is 3.27 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹. Calculate the ionization energy of hydrogen in kJ mol⁻¹.

E = hf = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.27 × 10¹⁵ = 2.17 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom.
IE = 2.17 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 6.02 × 10²³ ÷ 1000 = 1.31 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹ (1305 unrounded).

The convergence limit for vanadium is quoted as 54 411.7 cm⁻¹ (a wavenumber, 1/λ). Calculate the first ionization energy of vanadium.

A wavenumber is the reciprocal of the wavelength: λ = 1 ÷ 54 411.7 cm = 1.838 × 10⁻⁵ cm = 1.838 × 10⁻⁷ m (183.8 nm, in the UV).
E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) ÷ 1.838 × 10⁻⁷ = 1.082 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom.
IE = 1.082 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 6.02 × 10²³ ÷ 1000 = 651 kJ mol⁻¹, matching the data booklet value for V (651). (If 54 411.7 is mistakenly read as a wavelength in cm, the answer comes out absurdly small, about 2 × 10⁻⁷ kJ mol⁻¹: a sign that something is wrong.)
Worked example from class: helium's emission spectrum

Helium's visible lines extend down to about 390 nm, but its spectrum continues into the UV, converging at about 50 nm (more precisely 50.4 nm).

E = hc/λ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 2.998 × 10⁸) ÷ 50.4 × 10⁻⁹ = 3.94 × 10⁻¹⁸ J per atom.
IE = 3.94 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 6.022 × 10²³ ÷ 1000 = 2.37 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹, matching the data booklet value of 2372 kJ mol⁻¹. (Using a rounded 50 nm gives 3.97 × 10⁻¹⁸ J and about 2.39 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹.)

Finding the convergence limit from a graph AHL

The frequencies of the lines in the Lyman series are known. Every transition involves an electron falling from n ≥ 2 to n = 1. The difference in frequency between successive lines, Δν, shrinks towards zero as the lines converge.

The points fit an approximate straight line, Δν = −0.5897ν + 19.022 (in units of 10¹⁴ s⁻¹). At convergence Δν = 0, so ν = 19.022 ÷ 0.5897 = 32.26 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹. This gives IE = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.226 × 10¹⁵ × 6.02 × 10²³ ÷ 1000 ≈ 1.29 × 10³ kJ mol⁻¹, slightly low, because the true relationship is curved and a straight line is only an approximation. A better curve fit gives the intercept ν = 32.883 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹, and then:

IE = 32.883 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹ × 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ ÷ 1000 = 1312 kJ mol⁻¹

which agrees with the value in section 8 of the IB data booklet (H: 1312 kJ mol⁻¹).

Exam question(a) Hydrogen spectral data give the frequency 3.28 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹ for its convergence limit. Calculate the ionization energy, in J, for a single atom of hydrogen. (b) Calculate the wavelength, in m, for the electron transition corresponding to this frequency.

Part (b): calculate the wavelength corresponding to 3.28 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹.

Part (a): E = hν = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s × 3.28 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹ = 2.17 × 10⁻¹⁸ J [1 mark].
Part (b): λ = c/ν = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ ÷ 3.28 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹ = 9.15 × 10⁻⁸ m [1 mark].

title: Ionization energy trends and successive ionization energies
